notes: The Crane K is for fully turbulent flow; it is not valid in laminar flow (fluids docstrings): there it underestimates the loss, and it is flagged.
Open (status 'active'): the loss is the fully open K.

assumptions: Steady, incompressible, isothermal, single-phase liquid flow.
Reservoirs and reference nodes are quiescent bodies of liquid (velocity 0) at a constant head.

No entrance or exit loss is applied where a pipe meets a reservoir or reference node unless the connection's piping has an entrance fitting (entrance_sharp, entrance_rounded, entrance_projecting) or an exit fitting (exit); without one, the EGL at the port equals the boundary head in either flow direction. The web app adds a sharp-edged entrance where new piping leaves a reservoir and an exit where it enters one (removable), and none at a reference node; each boundary's trace lists the entrance and exit fittings at its ports.
Fluid properties are constant at the operating temperature.
Pumps have an integral check: no reverse flow.
Check valves: a disc that opens fully above the cracking pressure and closes on reverse flow (no partial opening).
Control valves without an entered resistance are ideal: no loss when fully open.
Fittings and valves without a user K use the cited correlation for the type at the connected pipe's inner diameter.

items: Global Gradient Algorithm (Todini & Pilati 1988): Newton's method on the energy grade line at every node and the flow in every link; sparse direct solve of the Schur complement (SciPy SuperLU, splu). One solver for every topology; every connected part needs a reservoir or reference node.

Converged when the largest flow change is at most the project tolerance times the largest flow (plus 1e-14 m³/s), continuity closes at every node and over every component to 1e-09 x the largest flow + 1e-14 m³/s, and the energy equation holds on every link to 1e-07 m. On each link, 8.88178e-16 x the largest magnitude among the energy grade lines at its two ends and its head loss is added to that tolerance (4 x 2.22045e-16, the machine epsilon of double precision): an allowance for the round-off of the heads that the energy residual subtracts, larger than 1e-07 m only where that magnitude exceeds 1e-07 m divided by that factor, about 1.1259e+08 m.

An active PRV or PSV holds its port's head and passes the flow of the pipe on that port, coupled exactly in Newton's step (EPANET 2.2 lags it by one iteration, which converges the same answer more slowly).
This project: friction method 'colebrook', flow tolerance 1e-09 (relative to the largest flow), at most 100 Newton iterations per network solve.
This solve: 6 Newton iterations in 1 outer iteration(s); converged.

Branch components (tees, wyes) are imposed exactly: each one's ports share one head unknown, offset by the branch's path losses (zero for an ideal junction), and its internal flows follow from continuity.

Flows below 1e-12 x the largest flow (plus 1e-14 m³/s) are round-off and reported as zero. Dead-end branches (no way out but the node they hang from) carry no flow by continuity and are reported as exactly zero.

Outer loop for statuses and branch losses: at most 30 counted iterations; an iteration that only holds or releases branch legs at zero flow is not counted (each branch is held a bounded number of times). Once pump and valve statuses repeat after an iteration that changed several of them, one status changes per iteration; a status pattern that still repeats goes back to the latest iteration that asked for several changes and takes one not yet taken, and with none left is reported as not converged, naming the elements that oscillate.
Parts of the network closed off from every reservoir and reference node by closed elements carry no flow and have no computed pressure (flagged).

A closed-off part that cannot carry zero flow (a pump loop behind a closed valve) has determined flows but no pressure level: its flows and head differences are solved with one node held at an arbitrary head, and its pressures, NPSH available and PRV/PSV setpoint checks are not reported (flagged).
references: Todini, E., and S. Pilati. A gradient algorithm for the analysis of pipe networks. Computer Applications in Water Supply, Vol. 1. Wiley, 1988, 1-20.
sections.title: Network solution

items: Darcy–Weisbach head loss h = f (L/D) v²/(2g), g = 9.80665 m/s² (standard gravity, fluids.constants.g), Re = |v| D/ν.
Laminar, Re < 2000: f = 64/Re (Hagen–Poiseuille).
Turbulent, Re ≥ 4000: the Colebrook (1939) equation, solved exactly with fluids.friction.Clamond (Clamond 2009).
Transition, 2000 ≤ Re < 4000: cubic interpolation between the laminar and turbulent laws (Dunlop's method, as in EPANET 2.2); flagged as transitional flow.

Flagged outside the cited range: Swamee–Jain beyond its documented 5000 ≤ Re ≤ 1e+08 and 1e-06 ≤ ε/D ≤ 0.05; Colebrook beyond ε/D = 0.05, the largest relative roughness documented for its explicit approximations (fluids.friction.fmethods). ε/D ≥ 3.7 has no Colebrook solution and is rejected.

Pipe dimensions: ASME B36.10M / B36.19M and ASTM D1785 via fluids.piping; roughness: Farshad & Rieke (2006) via fluids.friction.roughness_Farshad; user values where entered (each element's trace names its sources).
references: Swamee, P. K., and A. K. Jain. J. Hydraulics Div. ASCE 102(5), 1976, 657-664.
Rossman, L. A., et al. EPANET 2.2 User Manual. US EPA, 2020 (source: src/hydcoeffs.c).

sections.title: Minor losses

items: Tees and wyes with lossModel 'ideal' are junctions without loss, as in EPANET.

lossModel 'crane': the path losses follow the solved flow split with the Crane TP-410 tee and lateral correlations (fluids.fittings.K_branch_diverging_Crane, K_run_diverging_Crane, K_branch_converging_Crane, K_run_converging_Crane), K on the combined-flow velocity in the run diameter; updated in the outer loop until K changes by less than 0.0001 and the path loss by less than 1e-06 m.

A tee whose combined flow passes through the branch uses the Darby 3-K tee 'Tee, Through-branch, (as elbow), flanged, (r/D = 1)' per run path on its own velocity (flagged); a wye in that pattern has no cited correlation and is reported as not converged.

Flagged outside the correlations' range: a branch larger than the run (β > 1), unequal run pipes, a wye lateral turning against its lean, and a laminar combined flow (Re < 2000 on the combined-flow velocity in the run diameter: the Crane tee data are for turbulent flow).

Zero flow through a leg: the correlations for flow out through a leg and flow in through it give different port heads in the limit of zero flow. A leg whose flow reverses and reverses back between outer iterations is held at zero flow while the head the network gives its port lies between those two limits; its K is the one its head implies.

A flow split that keeps alternating across a step of a Crane correlation (a split at which the fluids function switches formula, q = 0.4, 0.5 or 0.6, and K jumps by more than 0.0001) holds K at the mean of the fluids values at the two splits while the solved split stays between them (flagged; the trace lists both values); a split alternating where the correlation is continuous has its K update under-relaxed instead.
references: Crane Co. TP-410 Flow of Fluids Through Valves, Fittings, and Pipe, 2009.
Silverberg, P., and R. Darby. Correlate pressure drops through fittings. Chem. Eng. 106(7), 1999, 101.
sections.title: Branches

items: Head, efficiency and NPSHr curves: monotone piecewise cubic interpolation (SciPy PchipInterpolator) through the entered points; head and NPSHr are extrapolated along the end slope outside the points (flagged), efficiency is held at its end values (flagged).
Speed: affinity laws, H(Q) = s² H₀(Q/s), NPSHr(Q) = s² NPSHr₀(Q/s), η(Q) = η₀(Q/s).
No viscosity correction: the curves are used as entered for the fluid (the Hydraulic Institute correction, ANSI/HI 9.6.7, is not in this version).
Integral check: a pump closes when the system head exceeds its shutoff head s² H₀(0) or the flow would reverse (EPANET 2.2 pumpstatus), and is flagged as flow reversal.

System curve of a pump: at each flow the pump is replaced by that fixed flow and the network solved, every other element following its own law and status rules (other pumps keep running); the system head is EGL(discharge) − EGL(suction). Default flows: 0 to 1.2 x the curve's largest flow x s. Each point starts from the solution at the neighbouring flow (statuses, branch losses and flows; the first from the network's own solve when the solve computes the curves, from the initial state otherwise), so where the statuses or branch patterns admit more than one solution the curve follows one continuously; a point that fails from there is solved from the initial state, and one that still has no head while the flow has a way through (unless a control valve in series is at its switch, below) is solved again from the initial state (if it did not start there) and from it with its active control valves open, the first solve that gives a head, or finds a control valve in series at its switch, being used (with none, the point keeps its first result) and the next point starting from the result used; a flowing point is not solved again when its flow exceeds what every way from the pump's discharge back to its suction can pass that way (an FCV at most its setpoint, a check valve, PRV, PSV or pump nothing in reverse: a cut, Ford and Fulkerson), since no steady state carries it, and one whose flow is that limit, where every steady state passes each FCV of the cut at its setpoint, is also solved with each such FCV held open, to find whether it sits at its switch. A point has no head where no steady state carries its flow, where its head is undetermined (a side of the pump with no fixed pressure, or a control valve in series at its switch, which could also hold the flow throttled with any higher head) or where its solve does not converge; its message says which.
references: Fritsch, F. N., and R. E. Carlson. Monotone piecewise cubic interpolation. SIAM J. Numer. Anal. 17(2), 1980, 238-246.

Fritsch, F. N., and J. Butland. A method for constructing local monotone piecewise cubic interpolants. SIAM J. Sci. Stat. Comput. 5(2), 1984, 300-304, doi:10.1137/0905021 (the derivative formula of scipy.interpolate.PchipInterpolator).
Rossman, L. A., et al. EPANET 2.2. US EPA, 2020 (source: src/hydstatus.c, status rules).

Ford, L. R., and D. R. Fulkerson. Maximal flow through a network. Canadian Journal of Mathematics 8, 1956, 399-404 (the max-flow min-cut theorem: the flows no state carries through a pump on its system curve).
sections.title: Pumps

items: Open valve loss h = K v²/(2g) on the inlet pipe's inner diameter; Cv and Kv converted with fluids.fittings.Cv_to_K / Kv_to_K (ISA-75.01.01, turbulent flow, without the Reynolds number factor F_R); without a resistance, the Crane TP-410 full-bore K for the valve type. A Cv, Kv or Crane K in laminar flow (Re < 2000 in the inlet pipe) is flagged.

Active check valves: open loss h = Δp_crack/(ρg) + K v²/(2g); open above their cracking head and close on reverse flow (EPANET 2.2 cvstatus with the cracking head). A check valve locked open by the user has the open loss K v²/(2g) only, with no cracking head and no check action; locked closed, it passes no flow.

PRV, PSV and FCV hold the outlet static pressure, inlet static pressure or flow when active; status rules from EPANET 2.2 (hydstatus.c) applied to the energy grade line, with the setpoint head z + p/(ρg) + v²/(2g) at the port; an FCV closes on reverse flow (EPANET's would pass it), and an active FCV opens once the head across it is below its fully open loss at the setpoint (EPANET's waits for a reverse head), as the PRV and PSV rules do. Control valves without a resistance: ideal control valve: no loss when fully open (K = 0); give a resistance for a real valve.
Status tolerances: 0.0001 m in head, 1e-08 m³/s in flow.

An active state with no solution falls back to the states the valve rules give at that solve's first iterations (EPANET 2.2 applies them at every iteration), then to open and closed valves (EPANET's badvalve).

A section closed off by closed pumps or valves carries no flow and has no computed pressure; the closed elements around it are re-tested against the heads it can take at zero flow (a dead-headed pump puts its shutoff head on it), and re-opened when no such head keeps them all closed. A PRV or PSV inside such a section or one whose pressure level is undetermined, or closed between two of them, keeps its state only if one set of section levels holds it together with those closed elements and the other such valves; otherwise the fewest of these elements change, each to the state its rule gives at levels that hold the others (a PRV or PSV that could not be active there, with no fixed head to draw from or deliver to, closes if open and opens if closed).
references: Rossman, L. A., et al. EPANET 2.2. US EPA, 2020 (source: src/hydstatus.c, status rules).
ISA-75.01.01-2007 (60534-2-1 Mod), Flow Equations for Sizing Control Valves.

NPSH available at the pump suction port = (EGL − z) + (p_atm − p_vap)/(ρg), the absolute static plus velocity head above the vapor pressure; margin = NPSHa − NPSHr, flagged as cavitation when negative.
Every port's absolute static pressure is checked against the vapor pressure (0 Pa absolute when none is known) and flagged where the liquid would flash.

sections.title: Atmosphere and NPSH

items: SI units throughout. Pressures are gauge unless labeled absolute; elevations and heads are measured from the single project datum.
Gauge pressures are relative to the atmospheric pressure: US Standard Atmosphere 1976 at the site elevation 0 m (fluids.atmosphere.ATMOSPHERE_1976).
The energy grade line EGL = z + p/(ρg) + v²/(2g) is the nodal unknown; the hydraulic grade line HGL = EGL − v²/(2g), with v the velocity in the pipe connected at the port. Pump head is the EGL rise.
Flow is positive from a connection's 'from' port to its 'to' port; branch port flows are positive into the component.
Every element's trace lists its inputs (with their source: user, default, library or computed), equations, correlations, data sources and intermediate values.
sections.title: Conventions

result.message: Every goal is met, after 10 evaluations.

items: Goal seek on the base case of this project: 1 variable(s) were varied within their bounds to bring 1 goal(s) to their targets. Each evaluation is a full network solve of the case with the variables set to trial values, by the methods in the sections below; nothing is approximated. The values found are not applied to the project: every result below is of the case with them, and applying them gives these results.

Method (one variable): the case's value, clipped into the bounds, is solved first, then the 9 values that divide the bounds into 8 equal steps (linearly), solved coarse to fine (the bounds, the middle, then the quarters and eighths). A value within a tenth of the tolerance ends the search, the one nearest the start when several are. Otherwise, where the residual (the goal's value minus its target) changes sign between neighbouring solved values, Brent's method (scipy.optimize.brentq, xtol 10⁻¹⁰ of the range, at most 200 iterations) searches the bracket nearest the start and stops at the first value within a tenth of the tolerance; a bracket that closes with both sides more than one tolerance from the target is a jump, and a bracket that ends at a jump or at failed solves gives way to the next. With no sign change among the values solved, the closest value is reported: on a plateau (neighbouring values solved within 10⁻³ of a tolerance of each other), at a bound, or refined by Brent's bounded minimization of the residual's magnitude (scipy.optimize.minimize_scalar, xatol 10⁻⁵ of the range) between the closest value's neighbours, where a sign change among the values it solves is searched as the scan's are. A crossing narrower than the scan's steps can be missed.

A goal is met when its value is within its tolerance of its target. The value reported is the nearest the start (in the scaled variables) among the values within a tenth of every tolerance, else among those within every tolerance; with none, the one with the least sum of squared residuals, each divided by its tolerance and rounded to 10⁻³ of it, the nearest the start on ties, then the earliest. An evaluation whose solve did not converge, that has no value of a goal, or whose trial values the network rejects (a topology or fluid-range error) is never used as a residual: the search goes around it, probing up to 4 times on each side of failed solves inside a bracket, and the closest-value search sees a residual of 10 times the largest so far, at least 1000 tolerances. At most 60 evaluations are made (60 for one variable), within the request's time budget of 45 s; an evaluation starts only while 1.5 times the slowest so far plus 1 s remains. An element's state counts as changed only when it carries more than 10⁻⁶ m³/s in one of the two states. A goal is noted as sensitive to a variable when rounding the value found to 6 significant digits moves it, at the slope between the two evaluations named, by more than its tolerance.
Variable 1: speed ratio of pump P1, bounds 0.5 to 1 (linear), start 1 (the case's value); found 0.868033.

Goal 1: flow in connection L2, target 0.0152 m³/s, tolerance 7.6e-05 m³/s (default: 0.5 % of the target (CLAUDE.md D6), at least the goal-seek default of 10⁻⁶ m³/s (D16, not in D6)); achieved 0.0152044 m³/s, residual 4.36668e-06 m³/s: met.
Stopped after 10 evaluations: Every goal is met, after 10 evaluations.
references: Brent, R. P. Algorithms for Minimization without Derivatives. Prentice-Hall, 1973, ch. 4 (scipy.optimize.brentq).

equations: H₀(Q₀): monotone piecewise cubic (PCHIP) through the rated-speed points; outside [Q₀,min, Q₀,max] the tangent line at the nearest end point
H(Q) = s² H₀(Q/s) (affinity laws at speed ratio s)
H = EGL_discharge − EGL_suction: the pump head is the EGL rise (total dynamic head)

H_sys(Q) = EGL_discharge − EGL_suction with the pump replaced by a fixed flow Q (system curve; other pumps keep running, valves follow their rules). Computed on request, at evenly spaced flows (default 0 to 1.2 × the curve's largest flow × s): POST /api/v1/system-curve, or with the solve when includeSystemCurve is set
No flow while EGL_discharge − EGL_suction > s² H₀(0) + 0.0001 m (the shutoff head) or the flow would reverse, Q < −1e-08 m³/s: the pump's integral check
P_hyd = ρ g Q H (hydraulic power)
p = ρ g (EGL − z_port − v²/(2g)): static gauge pressure at a port (z_port: the port's elevation; v: the velocity in the pipe connected there, Q/A of its end segment)
NPSHa = (EGL_s − z_s) + (p_atm − p_vap)/(ρ g) = p_s,abs/(ρg) + v_s²/(2g) − p_vap/(ρg) (s: suction port)

assumptions: Steady, incompressible, isothermal, single-phase liquid flow.
Reservoirs and reference nodes are quiescent bodies of liquid (velocity 0) at a constant head.

No entrance or exit loss is applied where a pipe meets a reservoir or reference node unless the connection's piping has an entrance fitting (entrance_sharp, entrance_rounded, entrance_projecting) or an exit fitting (exit); without one, the EGL at the port equals the boundary head in either flow direction. Fluid properties are constant at the operating temperature.
Pumps have an integral check: no reverse flow.
Check valves: a disc that opens fully above the cracking pressure and closes on reverse flow (no partial opening).
Control valves without an entered resistance are ideal: no loss when fully open.
Fittings and valves without a user K use the cited correlation for the type at the connected pipe's inner diameter.

items: Goal seek on the base case of this project: 1 variable(s) were varied within their bounds to bring 1 goal(s) to their targets. Each evaluation is a full network solve of the case with the variables set to trial values, by the methods in the sections below; nothing is approximated. The values found are not applied to the project: every result below is of the case with them, and applying them gives these results.

Method (one variable): the case's value, clipped into the bounds, is solved first, then the 9 values that divide the bounds into 8 equal steps (linearly), solved coarse to fine (the bounds, the middle, then the quarters and eighths). A value within a tenth of the tolerance ends the search, the one nearest the start when several are. Otherwise, where the residual (the goal's value minus its target) changes sign between neighbouring solved values, Brent's method (scipy.optimize.brentq, xtol 10⁻¹⁰ of the range, at most 200 iterations) searches the bracket nearest the start and stops at the first value within a tenth of the tolerance; a bracket that closes with both sides more than one tolerance from the target is a jump, and a bracket that ends at a jump or at failed solves gives way to the next. With no sign change among the values solved, the closest value is reported: on a plateau (neighbouring values solved within 10⁻³ of a tolerance of each other), at a bound, or refined by Brent's bounded minimization of the residual's magnitude (scipy.optimize.minimize_scalar, xatol 10⁻⁵ of the range) between the closest value's neighbours, where a sign change among the values it solves is searched as the scan's are. A crossing narrower than the scan's steps can be missed.

A goal is met when its value is within its tolerance of its target. The value reported is the nearest the start (in the scaled variables) among the values within a tenth of every tolerance, else among those within every tolerance; with none, the one with the least sum of squared residuals, each divided by its tolerance and rounded to 10⁻³ of it, the nearest the start on ties, then the earliest. An evaluation whose solve did not converge, that has no value of a goal, or whose trial values the network rejects (a topology or fluid-range error) is never used as a residual: the search goes around it, probing up to 4 times on each side of failed solves inside a bracket, and the closest-value search sees a residual of 10 times the largest so far, at least 1000 tolerances. At most 60 evaluations are made (60 for one variable), within the request's time budget of 45 s; an evaluation starts only while 1.5 times the slowest so far plus 1 s remains. An element's state counts as changed only when it carries more than 10⁻⁶ m³/s in one of the two states. A goal is noted as sensitive to a variable when rounding the value found to 6 significant digits moves it, at the slope between the two evaluations named, by more than its tolerance.
Variable 1: speed ratio of pump P1, bounds 0.5 to 1 (linear), start 1 (the case's value); found 0.868033.

Goal 1: flow in connection L2, target 0.0152 m³/s, tolerance 7.6e-05 m³/s (default: 0.5 % of the target (CLAUDE.md D6), at least the goal-seek default of 10⁻⁶ m³/s (D16, not in D6)); achieved 0.0152044 m³/s, residual 4.36668e-06 m³/s: met.
Stopped after 10 evaluations: Every goal is met, after 10 evaluations.
references: Brent, R. P. Algorithms for Minimization without Derivatives. Prentice-Hall, 1973, ch. 4 (scipy.optimize.brentq).
Brent, R. P. Algorithms for Minimization without Derivatives. Prentice-Hall, 1973, ch. 5 (scipy.optimize.minimize_scalar, method 'bounded').
Virtanen, P., et al. SciPy 1.0: fundamental algorithms for scientific computing in Python. Nature Methods 17, 261-272, 2020.
OpenSolve Pipe design decision D16 (CLAUDE.md), from docs/proposals/goal-seek.md.
sections.title: Goal seek

items: Global Gradient Algorithm (Todini & Pilati 1988): Newton's method on the energy grade line at every node and the flow in every link; sparse direct solve of the Schur complement (SciPy SuperLU, splu). One solver for every topology; every connected part needs a reservoir or reference node.

Converged when the largest flow change is at most the project tolerance times the largest flow (plus 1e-14 m³/s), continuity closes at every node and over every component to 1e-09 x the largest flow + 1e-14 m³/s, and the energy equation holds on every link to 1e-07 m. On each link, 8.88178e-16 x the largest magnitude among the energy grade lines at its two ends and its head loss is added to that tolerance (4 x 2.22045e-16, the machine epsilon of double precision): an allowance for the round-off of the heads that the energy residual subtracts, larger than 1e-07 m only where that magnitude exceeds 1e-07 m divided by that factor, about 1.1259e+08 m.

An active PRV or PSV holds its port's head and passes the flow of the pipe on that port, coupled exactly in Newton's step (EPANET 2.2 lags it by one iteration, which converges the same answer more slowly).
This project: friction method 'colebrook', flow tolerance 1e-09 (relative to the largest flow), at most 100 Newton iterations per network solve.
This solve: 6 Newton iterations in 1 outer iteration(s); converged.

Branch components (tees, wyes) are imposed exactly: each one's ports share one head unknown, offset by the branch's path losses (zero for an ideal junction), and its internal flows follow from continuity.

Flows below 1e-12 x the largest flow (plus 1e-14 m³/s) are round-off and reported as zero. Dead-end branches (no way out but the node they hang from) carry no flow by continuity and are reported as exactly zero.

Outer loop for statuses and branch losses: at most 30 counted iterations; an iteration that only holds or releases branch legs at zero flow is not counted (each branch is held a bounded number of times). Once pump and valve statuses repeat after an iteration that changed several of them, one status changes per iteration; a status pattern that still repeats goes back to the latest iteration that asked for several changes and takes one not yet taken, and with none left is reported as not converged, naming the elements that oscillate.
Parts of the network closed off from every reservoir and reference node by closed elements carry no flow and have no computed pressure (flagged).

A closed-off part that cannot carry zero flow (a pump loop behind a closed valve) has determined flows but no pressure level: its flows and head differences are solved with one node held at an arbitrary head, and its pressures, NPSH available and PRV/PSV setpoint checks are not reported (flagged).
references: Todini, E., and S. Pilati. A gradient algorithm for the analysis of pipe networks. Computer Applications in Water Supply, Vol. 1. Wiley, 1988, 1-20.
sections.title: Network solution

items: Darcy–Weisbach head loss h = f (L/D) v²/(2g), g = 9.80665 m/s² (standard gravity, fluids.constants.g), Re = |v| D/ν.
Laminar, Re < 2000: f = 64/Re (Hagen–Poiseuille).
Turbulent, Re ≥ 4000: the Colebrook (1939) equation, solved exactly with fluids.friction.Clamond (Clamond 2009).
Transition, 2000 ≤ Re < 4000: cubic interpolation between the laminar and turbulent laws (Dunlop's method, as in EPANET 2.2); flagged as transitional flow.

Flagged outside the cited range: Swamee–Jain beyond its documented 5000 ≤ Re ≤ 1e+08 and 1e-06 ≤ ε/D ≤ 0.05; Colebrook beyond ε/D = 0.05, the largest relative roughness documented for its explicit approximations (fluids.friction.fmethods). ε/D ≥ 3.7 has no Colebrook solution and is rejected.

Pipe dimensions: ASME B36.10M / B36.19M and ASTM D1785 via fluids.piping; roughness: Farshad & Rieke (2006) via fluids.friction.roughness_Farshad; user values where entered (each element's trace names its sources).
references: Swamee, P. K., and A. K. Jain. J. Hydraulics Div. ASCE 102(5), 1976, 657-664.
Rossman, L. A., et al. EPANET 2.2 User Manual. US EPA, 2020 (source: src/hydcoeffs.c).
sections.title: Pipe friction

items: Fitting loss h = n K v²/(2g), K from the cited fluids correlation for the fitting type (data/fittings.json) at the reference pipe's inner diameter; a user K overrides it.
Crane TP-410 K values use the fully turbulent friction factor ft_Crane(D); they are not valid in laminar flow, and a Crane K in a laminar segment is flagged.
references: Crane Co. TP-410 Flow of Fluids Through Valves, Fittings, and Pipe, 2009.
Rennels, D. C., and H. M. Hudson. Pipe Flow: A Practical and Comprehensive Guide. Wiley, 2012.
sections.title: Minor losses

items: Tees and wyes with lossModel 'ideal' are junctions without loss, as in EPANET.

lossModel 'crane': the path losses follow the solved flow split with the Crane TP-410 tee and lateral correlations (fluids.fittings.K_branch_diverging_Crane, K_run_diverging_Crane, K_branch_converging_Crane, K_run_converging_Crane), K on the combined-flow velocity in the run diameter; updated in the outer loop until K changes by less than 0.0001 and the path loss by less than 1e-06 m.

A tee whose combined flow passes through the branch uses the Darby 3-K tee 'Tee, Through-branch, (as elbow), flanged, (r/D = 1)' per run path on its own velocity (flagged); a wye in that pattern has no cited correlation and is reported as not converged.

Flagged outside the correlations' range: a branch larger than the run (β > 1), unequal run pipes, a wye lateral turning against its lean, and a laminar combined flow (Re < 2000 on the combined-flow velocity in the run diameter: the Crane tee data are for turbulent flow).

Zero flow through a leg: the correlations for flow out through a leg and flow in through it give different port heads in the limit of zero flow. A leg whose flow reverses and reverses back between outer iterations is held at zero flow while the head the network gives its port lies between those two limits; its K is the one its head implies.

A flow split that keeps alternating across a step of a Crane correlation (a split at which the fluids function switches formula, q = 0.4, 0.5 or 0.6, and K jumps by more than 0.0001) holds K at the mean of the fluids values at the two splits while the solved split stays between them (flagged; the trace lists both values); a split alternating where the correlation is continuous has its K update under-relaxed instead.
references: Crane Co. TP-410 Flow of Fluids Through Valves, Fittings, and Pipe, 2009.
Silverberg, P., and R. Darby. Correlate pressure drops through fittings. Chem. Eng. 106(7), 1999, 101.
sections.title: Branches

items: Head, efficiency and NPSHr curves: monotone piecewise cubic interpolation (SciPy PchipInterpolator) through the entered points; head and NPSHr are extrapolated along the end slope outside the points (flagged), efficiency is held at its end values (flagged).
Speed: affinity laws, H(Q) = s² H₀(Q/s), NPSHr(Q) = s² NPSHr₀(Q/s), η(Q) = η₀(Q/s).
No viscosity correction: the curves are used as entered for the fluid (the Hydraulic Institute correction, ANSI/HI 9.6.7, is not in this version).
Integral check: a pump closes when the system head exceeds its shutoff head s² H₀(0) or the flow would reverse (EPANET 2.2 pumpstatus), and is flagged as flow reversal.

System curve of a pump: at each flow the pump is replaced by that fixed flow and the network solved, every other element following its own law and status rules (other pumps keep running); the system head is EGL(discharge) − EGL(suction). Default flows: 0 to 1.2 x the curve's largest flow x s. Each point starts from the solution at the neighbouring flow (statuses, branch losses and flows; the first from the network's own solve when the solve computes the curves, from the initial state otherwise), so where the statuses or branch patterns admit more than one solution the curve follows one continuously; a point that fails from there is solved from the initial state, and one that still has no head while the flow has a way through (unless a control valve in series is at its switch, below) is solved again from the initial state (if it did not start there) and from it with its active control valves open, the first solve that gives a head, or finds a control valve in series at its switch, being used (with none, the point keeps its first result) and the next point starting from the result used; a flowing point is not solved again when its flow exceeds what every way from the pump's discharge back to its suction can pass that way (an FCV at most its setpoint, a check valve, PRV, PSV or pump nothing in reverse: a cut, Ford and Fulkerson), since no steady state carries it, and one whose flow is that limit, where every steady state passes each FCV of the cut at its setpoint, is also solved with each such FCV held open, to find whether it sits at its switch. A point has no head where no steady state carries its flow, where its head is undetermined (a side of the pump with no fixed pressure, or a control valve in series at its switch, which could also hold the flow throttled with any higher head) or where its solve does not converge; its message says which.
references: Fritsch, F. N., and R. E. Carlson. Monotone piecewise cubic interpolation. SIAM J. Numer. Anal. 17(2), 1980, 238-246.

Fritsch, F. N., and J. Butland. A method for constructing local monotone piecewise cubic interpolants. SIAM J. Sci. Stat. Comput. 5(2), 1984, 300-304, doi:10.1137/0905021 (the derivative formula of scipy.interpolate.PchipInterpolator).
Rossman, L. A., et al. EPANET 2.2. US EPA, 2020 (source: src/hydstatus.c, status rules).

Ford, L. R., and D. R. Fulkerson. Maximal flow through a network. Canadian Journal of Mathematics 8, 1956, 399-404 (the max-flow min-cut theorem: the flows no state carries through a pump on its system curve).
sections.title: Pumps

items: Open valve loss h = K v²/(2g) on the inlet pipe's inner diameter; Cv and Kv converted with fluids.fittings.Cv_to_K / Kv_to_K (ISA-75.01.01, turbulent flow, without the Reynolds number factor F_R); without a resistance, the Crane TP-410 full-bore K for the valve type. A Cv, Kv or Crane K in laminar flow (Re < 2000 in the inlet pipe) is flagged.

Active check valves: open loss h = Δp_crack/(ρg) + K v²/(2g); open above their cracking head and close on reverse flow (EPANET 2.2 cvstatus with the cracking head). A check valve locked open by the user has the open loss K v²/(2g) only, with no cracking head and no check action; locked closed, it passes no flow.

PRV, PSV and FCV hold the outlet static pressure, inlet static pressure or flow when active; status rules from EPANET 2.2 (hydstatus.c) applied to the energy grade line, with the setpoint head z + p/(ρg) + v²/(2g) at the port; an FCV closes on reverse flow (EPANET's would pass it), and an active FCV opens once the head across it is below its fully open loss at the setpoint (EPANET's waits for a reverse head), as the PRV and PSV rules do. Control valves without a resistance: ideal control valve: no loss when fully open (K = 0); give a resistance for a real valve.
Status tolerances: 0.0001 m in head, 1e-08 m³/s in flow.

An active state with no solution falls back to the states the valve rules give at that solve's first iterations (EPANET 2.2 applies them at every iteration), then to open and closed valves (EPANET's badvalve).

A section closed off by closed pumps or valves carries no flow and has no computed pressure; the closed elements around it are re-tested against the heads it can take at zero flow (a dead-headed pump puts its shutoff head on it), and re-opened when no such head keeps them all closed. A PRV or PSV inside such a section or one whose pressure level is undetermined, or closed between two of them, keeps its state only if one set of section levels holds it together with those closed elements and the other such valves; otherwise the fewest of these elements change, each to the state its rule gives at levels that hold the others (a PRV or PSV that could not be active there, with no fixed head to draw from or deliver to, closes if open and opens if closed).
references: Rossman, L. A., et al. EPANET 2.2. US EPA, 2020 (source: src/hydstatus.c, status rules).
ISA-75.01.01-2007 (60534-2-1 Mod), Flow Equations for Sizing Control Valves.
Crane Co. TP-410 Flow of Fluids Through Valves, Fittings, and Pipe, 2009.

items: Atmospheric pressure: US Standard Atmosphere 1976 at the site elevation 0 m (fluids.atmosphere.ATMOSPHERE_1976).

NPSH available at the pump suction port = (EGL − z) + (p_atm − p_vap)/(ρg), the absolute static plus velocity head above the vapor pressure; margin = NPSHa − NPSHr, flagged as cavitation when negative.
Every port's absolute static pressure is checked against the vapor pressure (0 Pa absolute when none is known) and flagged where the liquid would flash.
references: U.S. Standard Atmosphere, 1976. NOAA, NASA, USAF, Washington, DC, 1976.
sections.title: Atmosphere and NPSH

items: SI units throughout. Pressures are gauge unless labeled absolute; elevations and heads are measured from the single project datum.
Gauge pressures are relative to the atmospheric pressure: US Standard Atmosphere 1976 at the site elevation 0 m (fluids.atmosphere.ATMOSPHERE_1976).
The energy grade line EGL = z + p/(ρg) + v²/(2g) is the nodal unknown; the hydraulic grade line HGL = EGL − v²/(2g), with v the velocity in the pipe connected at the port. Pump head is the EGL rise.
Flow is positive from a connection's 'from' port to its 'to' port; branch port flows are positive into the component.
Every element's trace lists its inputs (with their source: user, default, library or computed), equations, correlations, data sources and intermediate values.

equations: Q_in = Q_a: continuity at the port (Q_in: the flow into the node through its connection; with a supply, Q_a < 0, the connection carries the flow away)
EGL: solved with the network (the port is a free node: its pressure is a result, not an input)
v = |Q_in|/A: velocity in the pipe connected at the port (its end segment, area A)
HGL = EGL − v²/(2g)
p = ρ g (EGL − z_port − v²/(2g)): static gauge pressure at a port (z_port: the port's elevation; v: the velocity in the pipe connected there, Q/A of its end segment)
p_abs = p + p_atm (checked against the vapor pressure)

inputs.name: Assigned flow Q_a (positive: leaves the network, a demand; negative: enters it, a supply)

intermediates.name: Flow into the node through its connection Q_in

notes: Assigned-flow node: it fixes the flow at its port whatever the pressure there. It is not a fixed-pressure boundary: a part of the network that no reservoir or reference node reaches through open elements (cut off by a closed valve or a stopped pump, say) carries a nonzero flow only if the assigned flows there sum to zero, and then its flows are solved and its pressure level is not (UNDETERMINED_PRESSURE); otherwise no steady state carries them, and the solve is reported as not converged, naming the node. A zero flow there is a closed end (ISOLATED_SECTION).

dataSources.citation: user data (equipment datasheet): rated pressure drop ΔP_r, rated flow Q_r and rated fluid density ρ_r as entered; h_r = ΔP_r/(ρ_r g), c = h_r/Q_r²
dataSources.name: Loss coefficient c

equations: h_r = ΔP_r/(ρ_r g): the rated head loss
c = h_r/Q_r²: the loss coefficient
EGL_in − EGL_out = h = c Q|Q| = h_r (Q/Q_r)|Q/Q_r| (Q: flow inlet → outlet)
ρ g h = ΔP_r (ρ/ρ_r)(Q/Q_r)|Q/Q_r|: the pressure loss at the solved flow and the case fluid's density ρ
A = π D²/4, v = Q/A and Re = |v| D/ν in the end segment of the pipe connected at each port (ν = μ/ρ)
p_in = ρ g (EGL_in − z_in − v_in²/(2g)), p_out = ρ g (EGL_out − z_out − v_out²/(2g)): static gauge pressures at the ports
Δp_static = p_in − p_out = ρ g h + ρ g (z_out − z_in) + ρ (v_out² − v_in²)/2: the static pressure drop

inputs.name: Rated pressure drop ΔP_r (loss of total pressure, inlet → outlet)
Inlet pipe inner diameter (its end segment at the port)
Outlet pipe inner diameter (its end segment at the port)

intermediates.name: Rated head loss h_r = ΔP_r/(ρ_r g)
Head loss by the law c Q|Q|
Static pressure drop Δp_static = p_in − p_out

notes: The rated drop is the dissipative loss of total pressure between the ports (friction and form), without the static head between them: the law acts on the energy grade line, and each port's static pressure follows from its EGL with the velocity in the pipe connected there, so the static drop also holds the ports' elevation and velocity-head terms. A datasheet's static drop S between nozzles at different elevations or bores is entered as S − ρ_r g (z_out − z_in) − ρ_r (v_out² − v_in²)/2, with the ports at their real elevations.

The loss scales with density only. It does not account for a viscosity or Reynolds number different from the datasheet's: with a more viscous fluid, or at flows well below the rated flow, the real loss may be higher than this law gives.

Density ratio ρ/ρ_r = 0.9991037252: the case fluid (998.2071505 kg/m³) is lighter than the fluid the rating is for (999.102621 kg/m³), so at any flow the pressure loss is 0.9991037252 × ΔP_r (Q/Q_r)²; the head loss does not depend on the density.

dataSources.citation: Kv = 60 (m³/h at 1 bar) converted with fluids.fittings.Kv_to_K(Kv, D=1 m) (ISA-75.01.01-2007); c = K/(2 g A²) with A = π D²/4 at D = 1 m
dataSources.name: Loss coefficient c

equations: K = fluids.fittings.Kv_to_K(Kv, D) = 1.6·10⁹ D⁴/Kv² with D in m, and c = K/(2 g A²), A = π D²/4: the same for every bore D (K ∝ D⁴ ∝ A²), evaluated at D = 1 m
EGL_in − EGL_out = h = c Q|Q| (Q: flow inlet → outlet)
ρ g h = (ρ/ρ_w) · 1 bar · (Q/Q₁)|Q/Q₁| with Q₁ = Kv m³/h: the coefficient's rated point, 1 bar at Q₁ on water of density ρ_w = ΔP₁/(g c Q₁²)
A = π D²/4, v = Q/A and Re = |v| D/ν in the end segment of the pipe connected at each port (ν = μ/ρ)
p_in = ρ g (EGL_in − z_in − v_in²/(2g)), p_out = ρ g (EGL_out − z_out − v_out²/(2g)): static gauge pressures at the ports
Δp_static = p_in − p_out = ρ g h + ρ g (z_out − z_in) + ρ (v_out² − v_in²)/2: the static pressure drop

inputs.name: Inlet pipe inner diameter (its end segment at the port)
Outlet pipe inner diameter (its end segment at the port)

intermediates.name: Rated point: pressure drop ΔP₁ (1 bar)
Rated point: head loss h₁ = c Q₁²
Water density of the definition ρ_w = ΔP₁/(g c Q₁²)
Head loss by the law c Q|Q|
Static pressure drop Δp_static = p_in − p_out

notes: The rated drop is the dissipative loss of total pressure between the ports (friction and form), without the static head between them: the law acts on the energy grade line, and each port's static pressure follows from its EGL with the velocity in the pipe connected there, so the static drop also holds the ports' elevation and velocity-head terms. A datasheet's static drop S between nozzles at different elevations or bores is entered as S − ρ_r g (z_out − z_in) − ρ_r (v_out² − v_in²)/2, with the ports at their real elevations.
A Kv is a rated point on water by definition, 1 bar at Kv m³/h (water of 999.2974456 kg/m³ in fluids' conversion): its loss scales with ρ/ρ_w, and it needs no pipe diameter.

The loss scales with density only. It does not account for a viscosity or Reynolds number different from the datasheet's: with a more viscous fluid, or at flows well below the rated flow, the real loss may be higher than this law gives.

Density ratio ρ/ρ_w = 0.9989089383: the case fluid (998.2071505 kg/m³) is lighter than the fluid the rating is for (999.2974456 kg/m³), so at any flow the pressure loss is 0.9989089383 × ΔP₁ (Q/Q₁)²; the head loss does not depend on the density.

dataSources.name: Pipe 1 roughness

equations: A = π D²/4 and v = Q/A (Q: flow from → to; D: segment inner diameter)
Re = |v| D/ν (ν = μ/ρ: kinematic viscosity)
h_f = f (L/D) v|v|/(2g) per segment (Darcy–Weisbach; f: Darcy friction factor, L: segment length)
1/√f = −2 log10(ε/(3.7 D) + 2.51/(Re √f)) for Re ≥ 4000 (Colebrook; ε: absolute roughness), solved exactly
h_j = n_j K_j v_j|v_j|/(2g) per fitting (n_j: quantity, K_j: loss coefficient of one fitting, v_j: velocity in the fitting's reference segment)
Δh = EGL_from − EGL_to = Σ h_f + Σ h_j
notes: Pipe 1: turbulent, Re = 171773 ≥ 4000: Colebrook; ε/D = 0.0004507 ≤ 0.05, within the range documented for the Colebrook equation's explicit approximations.

Crane TP-410 K values use the fully turbulent friction factor ft_Crane(D); they are not valid in laminar flow (fluids docstrings): there they underestimate the loss, and a Crane K in a laminar segment is flagged.

equations: Σ Q_port = 0: continuity (port flows positive into the component)
p = ρ g (EGL − z_port − v²/(2g)): static gauge pressure at a port (z_port: the port's elevation; v: the velocity in the pipe connected there, Q/A of its end segment)
q = Q_branch/Q_c: the branch's share of the combined flow Q_c (the flow through the one port that carries all of it)
β = D_branch/D_run (D_run: pipe on the combined port)
v_c = Q_c/A_run, A_run = π D_run²/4: the combined-flow velocity
h_path = K_path v_c²/(2g): the loss between the combined port and each other port, K_path from the Crane correlation for the pattern
EGL_port = EGL_combined − h_path (diverging) or EGL_combined + h_path (converging)
notes: Solved flow pattern: diverging from run_inlet.

Correlation: Crane Co. TP-410 (2009) via fluids 1.3.1 fluids.fittings.K_branch_diverging_Crane, K_run_diverging_Crane (D_run = 0.07792 m, D_branch = 0.05 m, angle 90°); K on the combined-flow velocity in D_run.

assumptions: Steady, incompressible, isothermal, single-phase liquid flow.
Reservoirs and reference nodes are quiescent bodies of liquid (velocity 0) at a constant head.

No entrance or exit loss is applied where a pipe meets a reservoir or reference node unless the connection's piping has an entrance fitting (entrance_sharp, entrance_rounded, entrance_projecting) or an exit fitting (exit); without one, the EGL at the port equals the boundary head in either flow direction. The web app adds a sharp-edged entrance where new piping leaves a reservoir and an exit where it enters one (removable), and none at a reference node; each boundary's trace lists the entrance and exit fittings at its ports.
Fluid properties are constant at the operating temperature.
Pumps have an integral check: no reverse flow.
Check valves: a disc that opens fully above the cracking pressure and closes on reverse flow (no partial opening).
Control valves without an entered resistance are ideal: no loss when fully open.
Fittings and valves without a user K use the cited correlation for the type at the connected pipe's inner diameter.
Equipment losses scale with the square of the flow and with density from one rated point, a Cv or a Kv (constant K); viscosity is not corrected.

items: Global Gradient Algorithm (Todini & Pilati 1988): Newton's method on the energy grade line at every node and the flow in every link; sparse direct solve of the Schur complement (SciPy SuperLU, splu). One solver for every topology; every connected part needs a reservoir or reference node.

Converged when the largest flow change is at most the project tolerance times the largest flow (plus 1e-14 m³/s), continuity closes at every node and over every component to 1e-09 x the largest flow + 1e-14 m³/s, and the energy equation holds on every link to 1e-07 m. On each link, 8.88178e-16 x the largest magnitude among the energy grade lines at its two ends and its head loss is added to that tolerance (4 x 2.22045e-16, the machine epsilon of double precision): an allowance for the round-off of the heads that the energy residual subtracts, larger than 1e-07 m only where that magnitude exceeds 1e-07 m divided by that factor, about 1.1259e+08 m.

An active PRV or PSV holds its port's head and passes the flow of the pipe on that port, coupled exactly in Newton's step (EPANET 2.2 lags it by one iteration, which converges the same answer more slowly).
This project: friction method 'colebrook', flow tolerance 1e-09 (relative to the largest flow), at most 100 Newton iterations per network solve.
This solve: 10 Newton iterations in 2 outer iteration(s); converged.

Branch components (tees, wyes) are imposed exactly: each one's ports share one head unknown, offset by the branch's path losses (zero for an ideal junction), and its internal flows follow from continuity.

Flows below 1e-12 x the largest flow (plus 1e-14 m³/s) are round-off and reported as zero. Dead-end branches (no way out but the node they hang from) carry no flow by continuity and are reported as exactly zero.

Outer loop for statuses and branch losses: at most 30 counted iterations; an iteration that only holds or releases branch legs at zero flow is not counted (each branch is held a bounded number of times). Once pump and valve statuses repeat after an iteration that changed several of them, one status changes per iteration; a status pattern that still repeats goes back to the latest iteration that asked for several changes and takes one not yet taken, and with none left is reported as not converged, naming the elements that oscillate.
Parts of the network closed off from every reservoir and reference node by closed elements carry no flow and have no computed pressure (flagged).

A closed-off part that cannot carry zero flow (a pump loop behind a closed valve) has determined flows but no pressure level: its flows and head differences are solved with one node held at an arbitrary head, and its pressures, NPSH available and PRV/PSV setpoint checks are not reported (flagged).

Assigned-flow nodes fix the flow leaving the network at their port (a demand, positive) or entering it (a supply, negative), whatever the pressure there: a nodal demand in the continuity equations, as EPANET's junction demands; their pressure is a result. They are not a fixed-pressure boundary. A dead-end branch to one carries its flow. A part of the network that no reservoir or reference node reaches through open elements carries assigned flows only if they sum to zero (to the continuity tolerance): its flows are then solved and its pressure level is not (flagged); otherwise the closed elements around that part whose status rules open as its pressure falls (a net demand) or rises (a net supply) are re-opened; with none left to open, no steady state carries them, and the solve is reported as not converged, naming the nodes and the elements closed around them (EPANET: a disconnected system). A flow control (an FCV, or a speed-controlled pump) that alone feeds assigned-flow nodes taking its setpoint flow leaves the pressure between them undetermined (reported as not converged, naming them); with another flow the node's flow passes and the control's rules take it to a limit (an FCV fully open below its setpoint, a speed-controlled pump at its maximum or minimum speed), or, above what the control can pass, or with reverse flow through it, no steady state carries it.
references: Todini, E., and S. Pilati. A gradient algorithm for the analysis of pipe networks. Computer Applications in Water Supply, Vol. 1. Wiley, 1988, 1-20.
Rossman, L. A., et al. EPANET 2.2 User Manual. US EPA, 2020 (source: src/hydcoeffs.c).
sections.title: Network solution

items: Darcy–Weisbach head loss h = f (L/D) v²/(2g), g = 9.80665 m/s² (standard gravity, fluids.constants.g), Re = |v| D/ν.
Laminar, Re < 2000: f = 64/Re (Hagen–Poiseuille).
Turbulent, Re ≥ 4000: the Colebrook (1939) equation, solved exactly with fluids.friction.Clamond (Clamond 2009).
Transition, 2000 ≤ Re < 4000: cubic interpolation between the laminar and turbulent laws (Dunlop's method, as in EPANET 2.2); flagged as transitional flow.

Flagged outside the cited range: Swamee–Jain beyond its documented 5000 ≤ Re ≤ 1e+08 and 1e-06 ≤ ε/D ≤ 0.05; Colebrook beyond ε/D = 0.05, the largest relative roughness documented for its explicit approximations (fluids.friction.fmethods). ε/D ≥ 3.7 has no Colebrook solution and is rejected.

Pipe dimensions: ASME B36.10M / B36.19M and ASTM D1785 via fluids.piping; roughness: Farshad & Rieke (2006) via fluids.friction.roughness_Farshad; user values where entered (each element's trace names its sources).
references: Swamee, P. K., and A. K. Jain. J. Hydraulics Div. ASCE 102(5), 1976, 657-664.
Rossman, L. A., et al. EPANET 2.2 User Manual. US EPA, 2020 (source: src/hydcoeffs.c).
sections.title: Pipe friction

items: Fitting loss h = n K v²/(2g), K from the cited fluids correlation for the fitting type (data/fittings.json) at the reference pipe's inner diameter; a user K overrides it.
Crane TP-410 K values use the fully turbulent friction factor ft_Crane(D); they are not valid in laminar flow, and a Crane K in a laminar segment is flagged.
references: Crane Co. TP-410 Flow of Fluids Through Valves, Fittings, and Pipe, 2009.
Rennels, D. C., and H. M. Hudson. Pipe Flow: A Practical and Comprehensive Guide. Wiley, 2012.
sections.title: Minor losses

items: Tees and wyes with lossModel 'ideal' are junctions without loss, as in EPANET.

lossModel 'crane': the path losses follow the solved flow split with the Crane TP-410 tee and lateral correlations (fluids.fittings.K_branch_diverging_Crane, K_run_diverging_Crane, K_branch_converging_Crane, K_run_converging_Crane), K on the combined-flow velocity in the run diameter; updated in the outer loop until K changes by less than 0.0001 and the path loss by less than 1e-06 m.

A tee whose combined flow passes through the branch uses the Darby 3-K tee 'Tee, Through-branch, (as elbow), flanged, (r/D = 1)' per run path on its own velocity (flagged); a wye in that pattern has no cited correlation and is reported as not converged.

Flagged outside the correlations' range: a branch larger than the run (β > 1), unequal run pipes, a wye lateral turning against its lean, and a laminar combined flow (Re < 2000 on the combined-flow velocity in the run diameter: the Crane tee data are for turbulent flow).

Zero flow through a leg: the correlations for flow out through a leg and flow in through it give different port heads in the limit of zero flow. A leg whose flow reverses and reverses back between outer iterations is held at zero flow while the head the network gives its port lies between those two limits; its K is the one its head implies.

A flow split that keeps alternating across a step of a Crane correlation (a split at which the fluids function switches formula, q = 0.4, 0.5 or 0.6, and K jumps by more than 0.0001) holds K at the mean of the fluids values at the two splits while the solved split stays between them (flagged; the trace lists both values); a split alternating where the correlation is continuous has its K update under-relaxed instead.
references: Crane Co. TP-410 Flow of Fluids Through Valves, Fittings, and Pipe, 2009.
Silverberg, P., and R. Darby. Correlate pressure drops through fittings. Chem. Eng. 106(7), 1999, 101.
sections.title: Branches

items: Head, efficiency and NPSHr curves: monotone piecewise cubic interpolation (SciPy PchipInterpolator) through the entered points; head and NPSHr are extrapolated along the end slope outside the points (flagged), efficiency is held at its end values (flagged).
Speed: affinity laws, H(Q) = s² H₀(Q/s), NPSHr(Q) = s² NPSHr₀(Q/s), η(Q) = η₀(Q/s).
No viscosity correction: the curves are used as entered for the fluid (the Hydraulic Institute correction, ANSI/HI 9.6.7, is not in this version).
Integral check: a pump closes when the system head exceeds its shutoff head s² H₀(0) or the flow would reverse (EPANET 2.2 pumpstatus), and is flagged as flow reversal.

System curve of a pump: at each flow the pump is replaced by that fixed flow and the network solved, every other element following its own law and status rules (other pumps keep running); the system head is EGL(discharge) − EGL(suction). Default flows: 0 to 1.2 x the curve's largest flow x s. Each point starts from the solution at the neighbouring flow (statuses, branch losses and flows; the first from the network's own solve when the solve computes the curves, from the initial state otherwise), so where the statuses or branch patterns admit more than one solution the curve follows one continuously; a point that fails from there is solved from the initial state, and one that still has no head while the flow has a way through (unless a control valve in series is at its switch, below) is solved again from the initial state (if it did not start there) and from it with its active control valves open, the first solve that gives a head, or finds a control valve in series at its switch, being used (with none, the point keeps its first result) and the next point starting from the result used; a flowing point is not solved again when its flow exceeds what every way from the pump's discharge back to its suction can pass that way (an FCV at most its setpoint, a check valve, PRV, PSV or pump nothing in reverse: a cut, Ford and Fulkerson), since no steady state carries it, and one whose flow is that limit, where every steady state passes each FCV of the cut at its setpoint, is also solved with each such FCV held open, to find whether it sits at its switch. A point has no head where no steady state carries its flow, where its head is undetermined (a side of the pump with no fixed pressure, or a control valve in series at its switch, which could also hold the flow throttled with any higher head) or where its solve does not converge; its message says which. With assigned-flow nodes, the cut counts their flows as fixed demands and supplies (Gale): a demand on the pump's side of the cut takes part of the forced flow, and one beyond it adds to what the cut must pass. Read the other way, the cut bounds the flow from below: a flowing point below the least flow that assigned flows need through the pump (a demand on its discharge side that a one-way element keeps every reservoir and reference node from feeding, or a supply on its suction side that one keeps from draining) has no steady state either and is not solved again, and one at that floor is solved with each FCV of the cut held open too. A side of the pump that reaches only assigned-flow nodes has no point with a head.

Fritsch, F. N., and J. Butland. A method for constructing local monotone piecewise cubic interpolants. SIAM J. Sci. Stat. Comput. 5(2), 1984, 300-304, doi:10.1137/0905021 (the derivative formula of scipy.interpolate.PchipInterpolator).

Ford, L. R., and D. R. Fulkerson. Maximal flow through a network. Canadian Journal of Mathematics 8, 1956, 399-404 (the max-flow min-cut theorem: the flows no state carries through a pump on its system curve).

Gale, D. A theorem on flows in networks. Pacific Journal of Mathematics 7(2), 1957, 1073-1082 (a flow with fixed supplies and demands exists when no node set holds more net supply than its cut can pass: the assigned flows in a pump's system-curve bounds).
sections.title: Pumps

items: Open valve loss h = K v²/(2g) on the inlet pipe's inner diameter; Cv and Kv converted with fluids.fittings.Cv_to_K / Kv_to_K (ISA-75.01.01, turbulent flow, without the Reynolds number factor F_R); without a resistance, the Crane TP-410 full-bore K for the valve type. A Cv, Kv or Crane K in laminar flow (Re < 2000 in the inlet pipe) is flagged.

Active check valves: open loss h = Δp_crack/(ρg) + K v²/(2g); open above their cracking head and close on reverse flow (EPANET 2.2 cvstatus with the cracking head). A check valve locked open by the user has the open loss K v²/(2g) only, with no cracking head and no check action; locked closed, it passes no flow.

PRV, PSV and FCV hold the outlet static pressure, inlet static pressure or flow when active; status rules from EPANET 2.2 (hydstatus.c) applied to the energy grade line, with the setpoint head z + p/(ρg) + v²/(2g) at the port; an FCV closes on reverse flow (EPANET's would pass it), and an active FCV opens once the head across it is below its fully open loss at the setpoint (EPANET's waits for a reverse head), as the PRV and PSV rules do. Control valves without a resistance: ideal control valve: no loss when fully open (K = 0); give a resistance for a real valve.
Status tolerances: 0.0001 m in head, 1e-08 m³/s in flow.

An active state with no solution falls back to the states the valve rules give at that solve's first iterations (EPANET 2.2 applies them at every iteration), then to open and closed valves (EPANET's badvalve).

A section closed off by closed pumps or valves carries no flow and has no computed pressure; the closed elements around it are re-tested against the heads it can take at zero flow (a dead-headed pump puts its shutoff head on it), and re-opened when no such head keeps them all closed. A PRV or PSV inside such a section or one whose pressure level is undetermined, or closed between two of them, keeps its state only if one set of section levels holds it together with those closed elements and the other such valves; otherwise the fewest of these elements change, each to the state its rule gives at levels that hold the others (a PRV or PSV that could not be active there, with no fixed head to draw from or deliver to, closes if open and opens if closed).
references: Rossman, L. A., et al. EPANET 2.2. US EPA, 2020 (source: src/hydstatus.c, status rules).

sections.title: Valves

items: Equipment (one side of a heat exchanger, a coil, a strainer, a filter, or another passive element given by its datasheet): the loss of total head from its inlet to its outlet is h = EGL_in − EGL_out = c Q|Q| (a loss of total pressure ρ g h), with c = ΔP_r/(ρ_r g Q_r²) from the rated pressure drop ΔP_r at the rated flow Q_r for a fluid of density ρ_r: a constant K, the square law of ISA-75.01.01-2007 eq. (1) for non-choked, turbulent liquid flow, and the high-Re limit of the 3-K method (Silverberg & Darby). The rated drop is the dissipative loss (friction and form) of total pressure between the ports, without the static head between them: each port's static pressure follows from its EGL with the velocity in its connected pipe, so the static drop reported is ρ g h + ρ g (z_out − z_in) + ρ (v_out² − v_in²)/2.

Density scaling: the pressure loss at the solved flow is ρ g h = ΔP_r (ρ/ρ_r)(Q/Q_r)², with ρ the fluid being solved. The operating density cancels out of the head loss h, which the rating alone sets; it only converts head to pressure.

A Cv or Kv rating is a rated point on water by definition (1 psi at Cv US gpm, 1 bar at Kv m³/h): c = K/(2 g A²) with K from fluids.fittings.Cv_to_K / Kv_to_K (ISA-75.01.01-2007, water at 999.29744568 kg/m³), the valves' conversion, evaluated at a 1 m bore; K ∝ D⁴ makes K/A² the same on every bore, so no pipe diameter is needed. Its pressure loss is (ρ/ρ_w) × 1 psi × (Q/Cv gpm)², or × 1 bar × (Q/Kv m³/h)².
Reverse flow (outlet → inlet) follows the same, symmetric law and is flagged: no datasheet rates reverse flow.
Laminar flow (Re < 2000) in the end segment of a connected pipe is flagged, as for a valve's Cv or Kv: the square law is the turbulent-flow law, and the loss is then likely underestimated.

At zero flow the law's slope 2c|Q| is 0: Newton's Jacobian uses at least 1e-06 x the slopes of the pipes at the element's ports there, as for every link that is not a pipe (EPANET 2.2 bounds such a gradient instead); the law itself is exact.

Viscosity is not corrected: the loss scales with density only. With a fluid more viscous than the rating's, or at flows well below the rated flow, the real loss may be higher than this law gives (a smooth-tube element dominated by friction scales as ρ^0.75 μ^0.25 Q^1.75 by Blasius' law); a correction needs the equipment's geometry or its vendor's own factors.
references: ISA-75.01.01-2007 (60534-2-1 Mod), Flow Equations for Sizing Control Valves.
Silverberg, P., and R. Darby. Correlate pressure drops through fittings. Chem. Eng. 106(7), 1999, 101.

notes: Assigned-flow node: it fixes the flow at its port whatever the pressure there. It is not a fixed-pressure boundary: a part of the network that no reservoir or reference node reaches through open elements (cut off by a closed valve or a stopped pump, say) carries a nonzero flow only if the assigned flows there sum to zero, and then its flows are solved and its pressure level is not (UNDETERMINED_PRESSURE); otherwise no steady state carries them, and the solve is reported as not converged, naming the node. A zero flow there is a closed end (ISOLATED_SECTION).

equations: H = z + h_L + p_s/(ρ g): the EGL held at every port (a body of liquid at rest; p_s: gauge pressure on the liquid surface)

notes: Quiescent boundary: the liquid level is constant and the liquid at rest (velocity 0); velocity head develops in the connected pipes.

No entrance or exit loss is applied where a pipe meets this boundary unless the connection's piping has an entrance fitting (entrance_sharp, entrance_rounded, entrance_projecting: the loss where flow leaves the boundary into the pipe) or an exit fitting (exit: the loss where flow leaves the pipe into the boundary). Without one, the EGL at the port equals the boundary head H in either flow direction: the velocity head v²/(2g) of the connected pipe is gained on entry and given back on exit with no loss. Such a fitting is a loss of its connection (see that connection's trace). The web app adds a sharp-edged entrance (entrance_sharp) where new piping leaves a reservoir and an exit where it enters one, which the user can remove; it adds none at a reference node.
Port port_1, connection 'L1': its piping has entrance fitting(s) entrance_sharp.
Port port_2, connection 'L5': its piping has no entrance or exit fitting, so no entrance or exit loss is applied there.

Correlation: Crane Co. TP-410 (2009) via fluids 1.3.1 fluids.fittings.K_branch_diverging_Crane, K_run_diverging_Crane (D_run = 0.07792 m, D_branch = 0.05 m, angle 90°); K on the combined-flow velocity in D_run.

assumptions: Steady, incompressible, isothermal, single-phase liquid flow.
Reservoirs and reference nodes are quiescent bodies of liquid (velocity 0) at a constant head.

No entrance or exit loss is applied where a pipe meets a reservoir or reference node unless the connection's piping has an entrance fitting (entrance_sharp, entrance_rounded, entrance_projecting) or an exit fitting (exit); without one, the EGL at the port equals the boundary head in either flow direction. The web app adds a sharp-edged entrance where new piping leaves a reservoir and an exit where it enters one (removable), and none at a reference node; each boundary's trace lists the entrance and exit fittings at its ports.
Fluid properties are constant at the operating temperature.
Pumps have an integral check: no reverse flow.
Check valves: a disc that opens fully above the cracking pressure and closes on reverse flow (no partial opening).
Control valves without an entered resistance are ideal: no loss when fully open.
Fittings and valves without a user K use the cited correlation for the type at the connected pipe's inner diameter.
Equipment losses scale with the square of the flow and with density from one rated point, a Cv or a Kv (constant K); viscosity is not corrected.
